Article Title: Three women stranded by a nationwide US flight shutdown bought a $48,000 Ford Bronco in North Carolina and drove 27 hours to North Dakota after failing to find a rental car, train or bus home
Article Text:
They had travelled to Charlotte, North Carolina, for a work-related training programme and were preparing to fly home.

No rental cars, buses or trains available

They bought a $48,000 Ford Bronco in less than two hours

A 27-hour drive across nearly 1,500 miles

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

The family has decided to keep the Bronco

When a nationwide flight shutdown left three women stranded at an airport in North Carolina, they spent more than an hour trying to find another way home. Rental cars were unavailable, buses were sold out and trains were not an option. Their eventual solution was unusual: they bought a brand-new Ford Bronco for $48,000 and drove nearly 1,500 miles to North Dakota.The group included Tara Harding, a nurse practitioner and clinic owner from Bismarck, North Dakota, and two of her employees, Maressia Cowger and Alisha Maier. They had travelled to Charlotte, North Carolina, for a work-related training programme and were preparing to fly home when the disruption began on November 13.According to a report by CBS News, their flights were rescheduled four times before being cancelled. The three women eventually decided that waiting for another flight was no longer practical.Harding told CBS that her decision was not just about getting herself home. Her two employees had children waiting for them, and the clinic had patients scheduled for Monday morning.According to CBS News, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) had ordered a nationwide ground stop on November 13 after problems involving radar data and communications disrupted air traffic across the United States.The order halted flights for more than four hours and left thousands of travellers dealing with cancellations and delays.The women initially tried to rearrange their journey through Delta Air Lines. But after repeated changes to their flight bookings, they began looking at road and rail options. Harding said they searched for rental cars but found none available within a four-hour radius of Charlotte. Greyhound buses were sold out, and they could not find a suitable Amtrak train or an Uber ride for the long journey to North Dakota.After more than an hour of trying to arrange transport, Harding called her husband. He passed on an idea suggested by his mother: why not buy a car and drive home? The women contacted a nearby Ford dealership. A salesperson agreed to keep the dealership open while they made their way there from Charlotte Douglas International Airport in an Uber.The group reached the dealership at around 7.45 pm. Less than two hours later, they drove away in a new Ford Bronco priced at $48,000. Harding described the purchase as an unexpected decision that happened very quickly. In an interview with NBC News, she recalled being on a three-way call with her husband, the car dealer and her employees as the group tried to work out whether they were really going ahead with the purchase.The choice of vehicle was also made under time pressure. Harding and her husband discussed buying something that would have a good resale value, since she initially considered selling it after reaching North Dakota. Her husband suggested choosing a vehicle they would enjoy driving if they decided to keep it. Harding, who describes herself as a Ford enthusiast, settled on the Bronco.Once the paperwork was complete, the three women began their journey from Charlotte to Bismarck. The drive covered approximately 1,500 miles and took 27 hours. They took turns driving and sleeping, stopping mainly at petrol stations and drive-through restaurants for fuel and food. The journey continued through the night, with the women sharing driving responsibilities so they could keep moving towards home.Harding told CBS News that she wanted to get her employees back to their families and be ready for patients at her clinic on Monday. The trip also gave the three colleagues an unexpected opportunity to spend time together outside work. Harding said they bonded during the long drive and had no regrets about the purchase.Harding had initially considered selling the vehicle once they reached Bismarck. But after the journey, she said she felt attached to it because of the circumstances in which they had bought it. Speaking to CBS News, she said she was now inclined to keep the SUV. Her husband also drove it several times after she returned home and wanted to retain it.The FAA disruption affected thousands of travellers. Around 18,000 flight cancellations had been recorded by Monday, according to media reports. The nationwide ground stop was the longest since the September 11, 2001, attacks.
Article Summary: Tara Harding, Maressia Cowger and Alisha Maier had travelled to Charlotte, North Carolina, for a work-related training programme and were preparing to fly home. They spent more than an hour trying to find another way home. Rental cars were unavailable, buses were sold out and trains were not an option. They bought a brand-new Ford Bronco for $48,000 and drove nearly 1,500 miles to Bismarck, North Dakota.

Article Title: A Texas couple sold their home with $259,490 in net proceeds, but a $150,000 second mortgage complicated the divorce payout; appeals judges cut the wife's additional monetary award from $92,426 to $18
Article Text:
The dispute centred on the sale of the couple's former marital home.

How the $150,000 mortgage led to the dispute

Why the appeals court reduced the award

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

A Texas appeals court has reduced a monetary award granted to a woman following her divorce, ruling that a lower court's calculation gave her more than she was entitled to under the original settlement.The Fourteenth Court of Appeals in Houston modified the judgment involving Charles Kimathi Murungi and Sarah Kawinzi on November 17, 2026, reducing the additional amount payable to Kawinzi from $92,426.44 to $18,369.25. The court, however, upheld the rest of the lower court's judgment as modified.The dispute centred on the sale of the couple's former marital home and a $150,000 second mortgage that Murungi had been ordered to repay himself.Murungi filed for divorce in October 2022. In 2023, he took out a $150,000 second mortgage, also referred to as the Discover Loan, to fund an agreed buyout of Kawinzi's share in the home's equity.Their divorce was finalised on May 31, 2024. Under the decree, the former marital residence was to be sold through a receiver, with the net proceeds divided equally between the two.The decree also specified that the second mortgage was Murungi's separate liability and that he was solely responsible for repaying it.If he failed to clear the loan before the house was sold, the receiver could adjust the distribution to ensure that the outstanding amount was borne entirely by him.However, the appeals court noted that Murungi had kept the entire loan amount in his personal bank account and used it for his own benefit instead of buying out Kawinzi's equity interest as agreed.When the house was sold in 2025, the net proceeds stood at $259,490.31. Since Murungi had not repaid the second mortgage, $148,114.40 was deducted from the sale proceeds to clear the outstanding loan and the property's title.This left $111,375.91 in the receiver's account.In November 2025, the trial court awarded Kawinzi the entire remaining $111,375.91, along with an additional monetary judgment of $92,426.44 against Murungi.Murungi challenged the calculation, arguing that it effectively made him liable twice for the same financial obligation.The appeals court agreed that the lower court had calculated the disbursement incorrectly.It said the original divorce decree entitled each party to half of the $259,490.31 net proceeds, or $129,745.16 each. Had Murungi repaid the second mortgage using his separate funds as ordered, Kawinzi would have received that amount.The appeals court ruled that awarding her $203,802.35 in total amounted to a windfall and violated the original 50-50 property division.It therefore reduced the additional monetary judgment to $18,369.25, bringing Kawinzi's total award to $129,745.16.The court dismissed five of Murungi's seven appeal claims, including challenges to the original property division, travel restrictions and child support calculations, saying it lacked jurisdiction to revisit the final divorce decree because he had not appealed it within the prescribed period.The modified judgment was affirmed.
Article Summary: The dispute centred on the sale of the couple's former marital home. Charles Kimathi Murungi took out a $150,000 second mortgage to fund an agreed buyout of Sarah Kawinzi's share in the home's equity. The couple's divorce was finalised on May 31, 2024.

Article Title: Greenpeace activists dumped around 15 tonnes of boulders into the North Sea, which have unexpectedly overlapped with a planned £12 billion windfarm project off England's coast
Article Text:
Image Courtesy: Andrew McConnell / Greenpeace​

Why is Greenpeace protesting?

Arctic Sunrise

What is Andy Burnham's offshore windfarm plan?

How did the boulders interfere with the project?

Two environmental priorities, one stretch of seabed

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Greenpeace activists have placed around 15 tonnes of boulders on the seabed off England’s east coast to prevent industrial fishing vessels from damaging marine habitats and threatening harbour porpoises. However, the underwater barrier has created an unexpected complication: much of it overlaps with the site of two planned offshore windfarms worth £12 billion, backed by the UK government and Andy Burnham.The boulders were placed as part of a campaign against bottom trawling, a fishing method that involves dragging heavy nets across the seabed. Greenpeace said the intervention was intended to protect a marine conservation area where fishing activity has continued despite its protected status. The organisation has since discovered that its chosen location also overlaps with plans for the Norfolk Vanguard windfarm development, raising questions about how the rocks could affect its construction.The incident has brought two environmental priorities into conflict: protecting marine ecosystems from intensive fishing and expanding renewable energy infrastructure.The protest centres on the Southern North Sea Marine Protected Area (MPA), a designated conservation zone along England’s east coast.The area is important for harbour porpoises, small marine mammals related to dolphins that rely on sound to navigate, communicate and locate food.The Southern North Sea supports nearly 20% of the UK North Sea harbour porpoise population. Its protected status is intended to reduce disturbances to the animals and maintain the availability of their prey. However, the designation does not prohibit every form of fishing throughout the area, and industrial fishing continues in much of the zone.Greenpeace has raised concerns about bottom trawling, a technique in which fishing vessels drag large, weighted nets along the seabed to catch fish living near the ocean floor. The equipment can disturb seabed habitats, damage marine ecosystems and capture animals that are not the intended target.The practice can also affect harbour porpoises indirectly. Intensive fishing can reduce the availability of fish on which the animals depend, while underwater noise from fishing vessels can interfere with their ability to locate prey using echolocation.According to Greenpeace's analysis , bottom trawlers recorded more than 37,200 hours of fishing activity in the Southern North Sea MPA in 2025, making it the most heavily bottom-trawled offshore protected area in the UK that year.The organisation argued that the continued activity undermined the purpose of the conservation designation. After announcing in June that it would take direct action if stronger protections were not introduced, Greenpeace deployed its vessel, the, to place large boulders on the seabed.Each stone weighed up to 2 tonnes. Dropped at strategic positions, the rocks were intended to obstruct the heavy nets used by bottom trawlers, making it difficult for vessels to drag their equipment through the designated area. Greenpeace said the barrier effectively closed around 116 square kilometres of the MPA to bottom trawling. It named the zone an 'Ocean Park' and planned to patrol the area to discourage other forms of industrial fishing.The action was also intended to draw attention to the gap between an area's official conservation status and the activities that are still permitted within it.The boulder operation took place just days before the announcement of a major offshore wind investment off the coast of Norfolk. The project, known as Norfolk Vanguard, is being developed by German energy company RWE in partnership with US private equity firm KKR.The £12 billion investment package will fund two offshore windfarms, Vanguard East and Vanguard West. The projects are expected to generate approximately 2.8 gigawatts of electricity, enough to supply around three million homes. The UK government is also contributing £1 billion through its state-owned National Wealth Fund. Construction is expected to begin in early 2027, with the windfarms scheduled to start supplying electricity by 2030.Andy Burnham has backed the investment, describing it as an important development for Britain's energy sector. The project is also expected to support around 2,300 jobs each year through its construction supply chain, alongside approximately 100 permanent jobs once the windfarms are operational.Offshore wind is an important part of the UK's plans to expand renewable electricity generation, reduce dependence on fossil fuels and strengthen domestic energy supplies. The Norfolk Vanguard development is among the country's largest planned offshore wind projects.The complication emerged when it became clear that most of the boulders Greenpeace had placed on the seabed overlapped with the area earmarked for Norfolk Vanguard East.The organisation had reportedly checked the seabed for existing cables, pipelines and shipwrecks before deploying the rocks. However, it was unaware of the planned windfarm development when it selected the locations. The boulders were placed without permission from the Marine Management Organisation (MMO), the government body responsible for regulating activities in English waters.The rocks could complicate the developers' preparations because offshore windfarm construction requires detailed surveys of the seabed. Developers need to understand the location of obstacles and assess the ground before installing turbine foundations and laying underwater cables. Unmapped boulders can therefore affect construction planning and may need to be relocated.RWE has begun discussions with Greenpeace to establish the precise locations of the rocks. The company is reviewing its existing seabed surveys and assessing whether the boulders could affect construction or the installation of undersea cables.The rocks are expected to be removed before construction progresses, potentially within the coming months. However, the extent of any disruption has not yet been established, and no confirmed construction delay has been announced.Greenpeace has maintained that the boulders should not present a significant obstacle, pointing out that offshore wind developers routinely move naturally occurring rocks from the seabed before construction. The organisation has also reiterated its support for offshore wind energy.The MMO has separately published the reported coordinates of the boulders, based on information Greenpeace relayed to HM Coastguard. The agency said it had not independently verified every position and advised fishing vessels and other sea users to take the locations into account when operating in the area.The incident highlights the challenges of managing increasingly busy marine spaces. The same stretch of ocean can be important for wildlife conservation, commercial fishing and renewable energy development, with each activity requiring different considerations.Greenpeace's intervention was intended to restrict a fishing method it believes is damaging a protected marine ecosystem. The Norfolk Vanguard project, meanwhile, is part of the UK's wider effort to expand renewable energy infrastructure. Although the two initiatives have different objectives, their geographical overlap has created a practical conflict.For now, the developers are assessing the location and potential impact of the boulders, while Greenpeace continues to argue for stronger protection of the Southern North Sea. How quickly the rocks can be removed and whether their placement affects the windfarm's construction schedule remain to be seen.
Article Summary: Greenpeace activists placed 15 tonnes of boulders on the seabed off England’s east coast to prevent industrial fishing vessels from damaging marine habitats. But the underwater barrier has created an unexpected complication: much of it overlaps with the site of two planned offshore windfarms worth £12 billion, backed by the UK government and Andy Burnham.

Article Title: Scientists studying a 200-million-year-old skull in South Africa have named a new dinosaur species whose young already weighed about 400 kilograms; microscopic bone evidence suggests the animal was st
Article Text:
Nyana rooiwalensis | Image Courtesy: WikiMedia Commons

Nyana rooiwalensis

Royal Society Open Science

A skull that had been hiding in plain sight

A heavyweight that was still growing

A missing piece in dinosaur evolution

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

They say growing up heavy gives you personality. We certainly hope so for this young dinosaur, that weighed 400 kg at barely three years old. For perspective, that is roughly the weight of a grand piano, and this prehistoric heavyweight was nowhere near finished growing. Scientists in South Africa have identified a previously unknown dinosaur species from a fossilised skull and other bones dating back more than 200 million years. Named, the dinosaur belonged to an early group of plant-eating dinosaurs whose descendants would eventually include some of the largest animals to ever walk the Earth. The findings, published in, add valuable information to our understanding of early dinosaur evolution.But its impressive size as a youngster is not the only reason researchers are interested in this discovery. The fossil is offering a glimpse into how early dinosaurs grew, evolved and eventually became giants.The fossil was discovered in 2018 near Qhemegha village in South Africa's Eastern Cape province. It was found in the lower Elliot Formation, a geological formation known for preserving fossils from the Late Triassic and Early Jurassic periods.The remains belonged to a juvenile dinosaur and included a remarkably well-preserved skull, along with parts of its spine, limbs and other bones. Measuring approximately 21.3 centimetres, the skull contained several important structures, including much of the braincase, the palate and the hyoid, a small bone structure associated with the throat.Researchers led by Atashni Moopen from the University of the Witwatersrand used powerful X-rays to examine the fossil and create a detailed three-dimensional reconstruction. The scans were carried out using the European Synchrotron Radiation Facility, which uses intense X-ray beams to reveal internal details without having to physically dismantle the fossil.By comparing the skull's anatomical features with those of other known dinosaurs, the team was able to establish that the remains belonged to a previously unidentified species.Well-preserved skulls from early sauropodomorphs rarely come by, especially in southern Africa. Having an almost complete specimen gives scientists more anatomical information to work with when studying how these dinosaurs were related to one another.While the skull helped identify the species, it was the dinosaur's limb bones that revealed just how unusual its growth was. Researchers examined thin slices of its fossilised bones under a microscope, looking for growth marks. Much like the rings found inside tree trunks, certain structures in dinosaur bones can provide clues about an animal's age and how quickly it was growing.The examination revealed at most two lines of arrested growth, which are marks left when bone growth temporarily slows down. Combined with the structure of the bone's outer surface, this suggested that the animal was still in an early stage of development when it died. Scientists estimated that Nyana was at least in its third year of growth. Despite its young age, its body mass was already estimated at approximately 400 kilograms.This figure was calculated by measuring the circumference of its thigh bone and comparing it with growth curves developed from related dinosaurs. In other words, researchers did not have a complete skeleton to weigh, but used the preserved bones and comparisons with other species to estimate its size.And it appears that Nyana was only getting started. By extending these growth curves, the researchers suggested that a fully grown individual could have reached a body mass of several tonnes. This remains an estimate rather than a confirmed adult size, since scientists have not yet found an adult specimen of the species. Its estimated body mass was more than four times that of similarly aged Massospondylus and Mussaurus individuals.Nyana belonged to a group called sauropodomorphs, which included some of the earliest ancestors and relatives of the enormous, long-necked dinosaurs that would appear later in Earth's history. The group eventually gave rise to giants such as Brachiosaurus and Diplodocus, known for their extraordinary size and long necks and tails. Unlike these later giants, Nyana probably walked on two legs.The discovery offers researchers an opportunity to investigate how the group developed the ability to grow so large. Its bone structure suggests that rapid growth was already taking place relatively early in sauropodomorph evolution, long before the appearance of the enormous sauropods that would become familiar to us.There may also be an interesting geographical connection hidden in its ancestry. Based on their analysis, researchers suggest that Nyana could have been closely related either to Sarahsaurus, a dinosaur discovered in North America, or to Ngwevu, another South African dinosaur. Its exact position on the dinosaur family tree is still uncertain, but either possibility could help scientists understand how these prehistoric animals were distributed across different continents.Nyana may never have reached its full potential, but even a youngster weighing 400 kilograms has managed to leave quite a sizeable impression on palaeontology.
Article Summary: The fossil was discovered in 2018 near Qhemegha village in South Africa's Eastern Cape province. It belonged to an early group of plant-eating dinosaurs whose descendants would eventually include some of the largest animals to ever walk the Earth. Scientists estimated that Nyana was at least in its third year of growth when it died.

Article Title: Arnold Schwarzenegger bought the M47 Patton tank he once drove during Austrian military service; the 46-tonne Cold War vehicle later became part of his Hollywood life and even featured in a Netflix st
Article Text:
Image: Tork Buzz

Arnold Schwarzenegger served as an M47 tank driver in Austria

Austrian Army dug up and restored the tank for him

Schwarzenegger drove his personal tank over a Mercedes-Benz for Netflix

What is the M47 Patton tank?

M47 Patton was used by several countries during the Cold War

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Schwarzenegger uses the tank to raise money for charity

Hollywood actor Arnold Schwarzenegger owns an unusual reminder of his early years, a 46-tonne M47 Patton tank that he once operated during compulsory military service in Austria. The actor served as a tank driver at the Belgier barracks in Graz between 1965 and 1966, when he was 18. Decades later, he purchased the same military vehicle from the Austrian armed forces and brought it to the US. The Cold War-era tank subsequently became part of his public persona and attracted attention through his association with it. In 2023, Schwarzenegger even drove the vehicle over a Mercedes-Benz in a Netflix promotional stunt, using his personal tank for the announcement of his role as the streaming platform's Chief Action Officer.Schwarzenegger completed his compulsory military service in the Austrian armed forces between October 1965 and June 1966. According to the Austrian Ministry of Defence, he was stationed at the Belgier barracks in Graz, where he served as a driver of an M47 Patton tank.During his service, Schwarzenegger also experienced an unusual accident involving the vehicle. Recalling the incident during a visit to his former barracks in August 2012, he explained that he had been conducting a routine check on the tank when he failed to notice that it was in reverse gear.The vehicle consequently moved backwards through the brick wall of a garage. Schwarzenegger later recalled the incident as a small accident from his military days.The Austrian Ministry of Defence confirmed that he eventually purchased his former tank from the armed forces in 1994.The story behind how Schwarzenegger recovered his former military vehicle is unusual. After his military service ended, the Austrian Army had buried the tank as part of a decommissioning process.According to Netflix Tudum, Schwarzenegger later contacted the Austrian military and expressed his interest in acquiring the vehicle. The army subsequently dug it up, restored it and transferred it to him.He eventually brought the tank from Austria to the US, where it remained part of his personal collection.Schwarzenegger has also spoken about using the tank's storage space to keep weights and dumbbells during his military service. He would work out between drills, continuing his bodybuilding training even while serving in the army.In May 2023, Schwarzenegger brought his M47 Patton tank into the spotlight through a promotional video announcing his appointment as Netflix's Chief Action Officer.The video showed the actor driving the 46-tonne military vehicle over a Mercedes-Benz outside Netflix's offices. The stunt was part of the streaming platform's promotional campaign for its 2023 action-film and television lineup.In an interview with Netflix Tudum, Schwarzenegger confirmed that he personally operated the tank rather than allowing a stunt driver to take control."Was it really me driving? Of course it was. I wasn't going to let someone else have that fun," he said.The stunt reportedly took just two takes, with the tank crushing two different cars during filming. A stunt team that had worked with Schwarzenegger for around 30 years supported the production.He explained that he was particularly keen to use his personal M47 because it was the exact same tank he had driven as an 18-year-old in the Austrian Army.The M47 Patton was an American medium tank developed during the early years of the Cold War. Its development accelerated following the outbreak of the Korean War in 1950, when the US Army sought a more capable armoured vehicle to counter newer Soviet tanks.The vehicle was developed by combining a modified turret from the T42 tank with the existing hull of the M46 Patton. It was equipped with a 90mm main gun and a stereoscopic rangefinder designed to improve targeting accuracy.According to The Tank Museum, production of the M47 ran from July 1951 to November 1953, with 8,576 units manufactured by the American Locomotive Company and the Detroit Tank Arsenal.The tank weighed approximately 46 tonnes and was powered by an 810-horsepower, 12-cylinder petrol engine. It could reach speeds of up to 30 mph (48 km/h) on suitable terrain and had an operating range of approximately 80 miles.It required a crew of five, including a driver, assistant driver, gunner, loader and commander.Although the M47's service with the US military was relatively short, the vehicle continued operating in several countries after being supplied to American allies.The US Army began replacing it with the M48 Patton from 1953, and the M47 was declared obsolete in 1957. However, several countries continued using the tank for decades.Its international operators included Austria, Belgium, France, Italy, Pakistan, South Korea, Turkey, Iran and West Germany.The vehicle also saw combat in several conflicts, including the 1965 India-Pakistan War, the 1967 Six-Day War and the Iran-Iraq War of 1980-88.According to The Tank Museum, Pakistan deployed M47 tanks against Indian forces during the 1965 conflict, including in the major armoured battles at Asal Uttar and Chawinda.Beyond its military history and Hollywood appearances, Schwarzenegger's M47 has also been used to support charitable causes.Netflix reported that the actor uses his personal tank to raise money for charity. The vehicle has become a distinctive part of his public identity, connecting his early military experience with his later career as an actor and public figure.Schwarzenegger has previously spoken about his attachment to the vehicle, particularly because it represents a period when he was balancing compulsory military service with his ambitions in bodybuilding.
Article Summary: Arnold Schwarzenegger served as a tank driver in Austria between 1965 and 1966. He purchased the M47 Patton tank from the Austrian armed forces in 1994. In 2023, he drove the vehicle over a Mercedes-Benz in a Netflix promotional stunt.

Article Title: A West Virginia woman lost data when a replacement laptop failed; after the company missed her lawsuit for 18 months, the state's top court left $15,507.92 in compensatory damages intact
Article Text:
The $20,000 punitive damages award faced appellate scrutiny over West Virginia default judgment relief limits.

A costly default after eighteen months of silence

High Court upholds compensatory award

Scrutiny over punitive damages

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

For any consumer who has ever watched a hard drive crash without a backup, losing years of personal files is a familiar nightmare, yet few expect that frustration to end in a multi-year legal battle reaching the highest court in the state. In a ruling issued by the Supreme Court of Appeals of West Virginia, technology giant HP Inc. failed in its bid to overturn a $15,507.92 compensatory damages award granted to a customer after both her original laptop and a warranty replacement broke down, erasing her stored data.The dispute dates back to July 2019, when West Virginia resident Ms. Thomas purchased an HP laptop at a Best Buy retail store for $1,527.98 and later added a three-year extended warranty, according to records reviewed by the Supreme Court of Appeals of West Virginia. When technical problems plagued the original computer and technicians could not fix it, HP provided a replacement machine under the warranty agreement. However, that replacement unit also failed roughly six months later, wiping out Ms. Thomas’s stored data and leaving repair technicians unable to restore it.Frustrated by the repeated hardware failures and seeking a purchase-price refund alongside compensation for unauthorized and excessive Instant Ink subscription charges, Ms.Thomas filed a civil lawsuit. HP never responded to the complaint for approximately eighteen months, an oversight the company later attributed to an internal misrouting of legal paperwork to an employee on medical leave, the Supreme Court of Appeals of West Virginia noted. In November 2022, a circuit court entered an amended default judgment awarding Ms. Thomas $15,507.92 in compensatory damages, covering the defective laptop, a replacement device, ink charges, and inconvenience, alongside $20,000 in punitive damages and $9,130.33 in legal costs and attorney fees.Once HP discovered the judgment and sought to set it aside under state procedural rules, the company argued that the lower court lacked jurisdiction because the initial complaint did not meet the financial threshold and contended that internal administrative error constituted excusable neglect. Both the circuit court and the Intermediate Court of Appeals rejected HP’s effort to erase the default judgment, prompting the company to appeal to the state’s highest bench.The Supreme Court of Appeals of West Virginia affirmed the decision to leave the default judgment and the $15,507.92 compensatory award intact. Reading the consumer’s initial complaint favorably, the justices concluded that Ms. Thomas had sufficiently alleged $10,000 in damages to establish the circuit court’s jurisdiction. Furthermore, the court determined that misrouting a lawsuit to an absent employee did not excuse an eighteen-month failure to appear in court, meaning HP failed to demonstrate the good cause required to reopen the underlying liability ruling.While the compensatory award survived intact, the litigation surrounding the $20,000 punitive damages component drew sharp scrutiny during appellate review. Under West Virginia civil procedure rules governing default judgments, a court generally cannot grant relief that differs in kind or exceeds the specific amount requested in a plaintiff’s original complaint. Although the Supreme Court of Appeals of West Virginia found that HP had waived certain appellate arguments regarding the punitive award by failing to brief them properly, the case sparked a notable dissent from the bench.One justice dissenting noted that Ms. Thomas never sought punitive damages or alleged facts warranting them in her initial filing. Any punitive damages beyond $10,000 in the complaint would violate procedural safeguards, the justice said. The majority's memorandum decision holds HP liable for compensatory damages and attorney fees from its prolonged courtroom absence.Image Courtesy: Google Gemini
Article Summary: HP Inc. failed in its bid to overturn a $15,507.92 compensatory damages award granted to a customer after both her original laptop and a warranty replacement broke down. The dispute dates back to July 2019, when West Virginia resident Ms. Thomas filed a civil lawsuit. HP never responded to the complaint for approximately eighteen months.

Article Title: In 1980, Billy Starr launched a Massachusetts charity bike ride; 46 years later, the Pan-Mass Challenge has donated more than $1.2 billion to cancer care, including a record $80 million presented on N
Article Text:
Billy StarrPhoto credit: Pmc.org

How the ride began

A record breaking gift

Where the money goes

Image: Canva

More than a weekend ride

A community built around a cause

Why the milestone matters

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

In 1980, Billy Starr launched a charity bike ride in Massachusetts with a simple idea: cyclists could turn miles into money for cancer research. Forty six years later, the Pan-Mass Challenge has become one of the world’s most successful athletic fundraisers, donating more than $1.2 billion to Dana-Farber Cancer Institute, according to Dana-Farber and CBS Boston.On November 15, the organisation presented a record breaking $80 million gift to Dana-Farber at a celebratory brunch in Boston. The amount exceeded the 2026 fundraising goal by $1 million and represents the latest chapter in a fundraising effort that has grown from a single ride into a year round community of riders, volunteers, donors, and corporate partners.Billy Starr founded the Pan-Mass Challenge in 1980. The event began as a bike a thon designed to raise money for cancer care and research, and Starr remains its founder and chairman.The idea was straightforward. Riders would raise money through their participation, and the proceeds would support Dana-Farber’s work through the Jimmy Fund, the institute’s community fundraising arm.Over time, the event expanded beyond a single weekend ride. It became a broader fundraising platform that includes indoor cycling, gravel rides, and children’s events, all connected to the same mission.The $80 million gift presented on November 15 was the largest in the Pan-Mass Challenge’s history.It surpassed the 2026 goal of $79 million by $1 million, according to CBS Boston.The donation brings the PMC’s total contribution to Dana-Farber to more than $1.2 billion. That figure reflects decades of fundraising rather than a single year’s effort.Starr said the money represents more than a number. He described it as funding for the next clinical trial, the next breakthrough, the next life saved, and the next patient who gets to ring the bell at the end of treatment.For the 20th consecutive year, 100 percent of every rider raised dollar goes directly to Dana-Farber. That model has helped the PMC become one of the most trusted names in athletic fundraising.The organisation says its support has helped drive recent breakthroughs at Dana-Farber, including the discovery of menin inhibitors, improvements in multi cancer early detection, and the development of new cell therapies such as CAR T and tumor infiltrating lymphocyte therapy.Dana-Farber president and CEO Benjamin Ebert, who is also a PMC rider, said the gift will help shape the future of cancer care and research at the institute. He described the donation as an important milestone and thanked the riders and volunteers who made it possible.The Pan-Mass Challenge is no longer limited to its signature two day ride across Massachusetts. The organisation has expanded into other formats that allow more people to participate throughout the year.PMC Winter Cycle is an indoor spin event held at Fenway Park. PMC Unpaved is a gravel bike ride, while PMC Kids Rides are mini bike a thons for children ages 2 to 15.These additional events help broaden the organisation’s reach. They bring in riders who may not be able to complete the main ride, while still contributing to the same fundraising goal.The Pan-Mass Challenge attracts riders and volunteers from 44 states and eight countries. It also draws support from more than 300,000 individual donors, according to Dana-Farber.The organisation says its success comes from combining the efforts of cyclists, volunteers, corporate sponsors, and individual donors. The goal is to maximise fundraising efficiency while increasing the annual gift.Starr said he has never been prouder of the PMC community. He argued that riders, volunteers, donors, and corporate partners understood what was at stake and helped push the organisation past its goal.The $80 million gift arrives at a time when federal research support and grant approval rates are shrinking, while cancer rates continue to climb. Dana-Farber says more than 20 million new cancer cases are projected worldwide in 2026 alone.In that context, the PMC’s sustained giving has become an important force for keeping research moving forward. The organisation’s support helps fund studies, clinical trials, and treatments that may not otherwise move as quickly.For the riders and volunteers who make the event possible, the milestone is a reminder that their work has real world impact. What began as a bike ride in 1980 has grown into a fundraising engine that continues to shape the future of cancer care.
Article Summary: Billy Starr founded the Pan-Mass Challenge in 1980. The event began as a bike a thon designed to raise money for cancer care and research, and Starr remains its founder and chairman. On November 15, the organisation presented a record breaking $80 million gift to Dana-Farber.

Article Title: Scientists tracked Manx shearwaters across the Atlantic for two decades and found that fast eastward flights can give birds jet lag; even experienced adults drift off course before correcting their ro
Article Text:
Manx Shearwaters, the marine birds that hunt over the open ocean Image credits: Oxford University

How a slow body clock sends birds the wrong way

Infographic showing clock-shift that occurs during homing flights of shearwaters. The bird begins to home at point A. On the first day of homing, its endogenous clock is calibrated to local time at 30°W. However, the shearwater travels eastwards to 15°W over 6 hours to point B. Here, sunrise happened an hour earlier, so the shearwater’s perceived time lags local time by an hour and the sun is roughly 20° further clockwise than the shearwater expects. At point B, this discrepancy causes the shearwater to orient roughly 20° clockwise of the correct direction. Image Credits: Credit: Lewin et al, 2026. Oxford University

Small errors for adults, bigger risks for first-timers

Manx shearwater in flight over sea Image credits: thelonekayaker/ wordpress

Manx Shearwater Puffinus puffinus Image credits: birdsoftheworld.org

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Manx shearwaters flying home from feeding trips can be nudged off course by a kind of jet lag, researchers say. It happens when a bird’s body clock falls out of step with the local time. Tracking data from Manx shearwaters on the west coast of the UK revealed that when the birds returned home to their colonies after trips over the Atlantic, their rapid eastward flights disrupted their sense of time and navigation.When humans get jet lag, we fly across time zones and feel tired and out of sync because our body clock is still running on the old time. Shearwaters seem to have a similar problem. For them, it shows up as a wrong turn over the open sea.A studyfinds that long-distance flights can throw seabirds' internal clocks out of sync, causing navigation errors , it was published in October 2026 on the Oxford University website. It talks about how researchers in Oxford University's Department of Biology analysed 20 years of GPS tracking data from 1,045 breeding shearwaters, covering 3,688 foraging trips. The birds set off from colonies on the west coasts of the UK and Ireland. Some flew about 1,000km west to find food. On the way home, they flew east, back to their nests.Like many animals, shearwaters use the sun as a compass. This is very useful over open water, where there are no roads or landmarks. But the sun moves across the sky during the day, so a bird needs to know the time to work out where the sun should be. The bird’s body clock gives it that information. It is called the circadian rhythm. Birds normally reset their clocks at sunrise. That works well while a bird stays in one place. But when a bird travels quickly east or west, its clock can fall out of sync with local solar time. On the flight home, the shearwaters crossed places where the sun rises earlier. The Oxford release says this can leave their clocks lagging behind local time by up to around one hour.The researchers worked out how a slow clock should change the birds’ sun compass. Then they compared those predictions with the directions the GPS trackers recorded. As the birds travelled east, they tended to drift clockwise from their expected direction. That is what you would expect if their clocks were running behind. The team from the Department of Biology found that when the predicted compass error pointed towards land, the shearwaters flew closer to the coast. When it pointed away from land, they flew further out to sea. So the birds seem to use the sun compass even when familiar land is close by.The errors were real, but they were small. In “Seabirds get jet lag, too — and it can throw them a bit off course,” published by Science News on October 29, 2026, Anirban Mukhopadhyay reports that the birds veered by as much as 15 degrees. The errors were small enough to add only a few kilometres to the journey. They were not enough to stop the shearwaters from finding their way home.Adult birds can fix their mistakes because they keep checking where they are. The Oxford team calculated that a shearwater returning from 1,000 km away with an average compass error of seven degrees would fly only about 5 km further than needed to get within 5 km of its colony.“It’s inherently difficult to study the cognitive processes of animals in the wild, so it’s exciting to realise that if we measure their natural movements carefully enough we can reveal the underlying behavioural mechanisms.” - Co-author Professor Tim Guilford, Department of Biology, Oxford University. The consequences could be more significant for animals that cannot continuously reassess and correct their positions.For example, young birds undertaking their first migration could be particularly vulnerable. Small navigational errors might accumulate over a long journey, potentially shifting their eventual destination by hundreds of kilometres.Researchers do not yet know whether the clock mismatch affects the birds in other ways. Internal clocks control many parts of an animal’s behaviour and body, so the problem could reach beyond navigation. More work is needed to find out. Dr Patrick Lewin, the lead researcher, has said that studying animals that regularly travel long distances could one day help us understand how humans cope with jet lag. “It’s amazing to think that billions of migratory animals look up to the sun for direction, relying on clocks silently ticking away inside them, and that errors in those clocks can cause them to take tiny shifts off course. ” - Lead researcher Dr Patrick Lewin, Department of Biology, Oxford University.
Article Summary: Manx shearwaters flying home from feeding trips can be nudged off course by a kind of jet lag, researchers say. It happens when a bird’s body clock falls out of step with the local time. For them, it shows up as a wrong turn over the open sea.

Article Title: Pennsylvania woman arrested after taking back her repossessed car, which police had listed as stolen; man driving it with her permission spent two weeks in jail
Article Text:
PC: AI Generated

How did Alburg driving her repossessed BMW away lead to a stolen-car report

Stolen-car database entry led to Edwards’s arrest and two weeks in jail

Police pursued theft charges against Alburg despite title listing her as owner

How did the court assess the police response to the car ownership dispute

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Disclaimer:

This article is based on a memorandum opinion issued by the US District Court for the Eastern District of Pennsylvania on 21 May 2025. The Times of India has not independently verified the facts or allegations presented by the parties. The claims, arguments, and court findings mentioned in this article are reported as recorded in the court opinion.

A Pennsylvania woman was arrested after taking her own car from a storage lot where a loan company had repossessed it. The company had seized the vehicle after she defaulted on a loan secured against it. However, the woman remained its registered owner, with the lender listed only as a lienholder.After she drove the car away, the storage lot owner reported it stolen, and a Pennsylvania State Police trooper entered it as stolen in a national crime database. Two weeks later, police arrested Timothy Edwards while he was driving the car with the woman's permission. In a memorandum opinion issued on 21 May 2025, the US District Court for the Eastern District of Pennsylvania examined the case. The woman, Ayana Alburg, was later arrested and charged with theft offences. Both subsequently filed a federal civil rights lawsuit against the officers and local authorities involved.Ayana Alburg had obtained a loan from Auto Equity Loans of DE, LLC, using her 2006 BMW X5 as security. The loan carried an annual percentage rate of 300%, which the court noted was illegal under Pennsylvania civil and criminal law. After Alburg defaulted, the company hired Top Notch Recovery, Inc.to repossess the vehicle for AEL.On 3 August 2018, Alburg went to Top Notch’s lot to collect her personal possessions. While the lot attendant and owner, Christopher Smith, was with another person, she drove her car away. Smith called the police and reported the car stolen. He told Pennsylvania State Police Trooper Elijah Jones that Top Notch had repossessed it on the loan company’s behalf.Trooper Jones entered the car as stolen in the national CLEAN/NCIC crime database. The entry identified Alburg as its registered owner and recorded that the registered owner had left with the vehicle. Two weeks later, on 17 August 2018, Timothy Edwards was driving the car with Alburg’s permission.Ridley Township Police Officer Timothy Kearney noticed a blue tarp covering the car’s rear window and checked its registration number in the CLEAN database. The search showed that the vehicle had been reported stolen. Kearney stopped the car and arrested Edwards. At the police station, Edwards was charged with receiving stolen property, unauthorised use of a motor vehicle, driving under a suspended licence and driving without a licence. He could not pay the $10,000 bail and remained in jail for two weeks.On 22 August 2018, Alburg’s lawyer wrote to Jones and Corporal Thomas Falcon, explaining that Alburg owned the car and had permitted Edwards to drive it. He also pointed out that AEL was a secured creditor seeking to recover a debt and that the police had to remain neutral in such disputes. Despite this explanation, Falcon later considered charging Alburg.An assistant district attorney advised that ownership was determined by the vehicle’s title, which listed Alburg as owner and Auto Equity Loans as lienholder. Falcon nevertheless decided that the loan company was the true owner and directed Jones to file a criminal complaint against Alburg.Jones’s complaint described the car as belonging to the company. A magisterial district judge issued an arrest warrant charging Alburg with theft by unlawful taking, theft by deception and unauthorised use of a motor vehicle. She was arrested on 4 February 2019. The Montgomery County Court of Common Pleas later dismissed the theft charges on 22 May 2019 and dropped the unauthorised-use charge on 13 September 2019.Separately, Edwards pleaded guilty to driving with a suspended licence in the Delaware County Court of Common Pleas on 12 February 2019. He was fined $200, while the theft charges against him were dismissed.The court said police were required to remain neutral in private disputes between creditors and debtors. It found that Jones had sided with the loan company by entering the car as stolen in the national database. However, it granted summary judgment to the officers on Alburg’s claims of illegal seizure and denial of due process. It refused to dismiss her false-arrest and malicious-prosecution claims, finding that disputes over the facts and witnesses’ credibility needed to be resolved.Detective Charles Palo drafted the criminal complaint against Edwards. The court also granted qualified immunity to Jones, Palo, and Kearney on Edwards’s malicious-prosecution claim. It did not make a final ruling on whether the officers were liable to Alburg. Instead, it left the questions of probable cause and the officers’ conduct for further consideration.
Article Summary: A Pennsylvania woman was arrested after taking her own car from a storage lot where a loan company had repossessed it. The company had seized the vehicle after she defaulted on a loan secured against it. After she drove the car away, the storage lot owner reported it stolen, and a Pennsylvania State Police trooper entered it as stolen in a national crime database. Two weeks later, police arrested Timothy Edwards while he was driving the car with the woman's permission.

Article Title: In 2005, Seattle began restoring neglected urban forests with volunteers; two decades later, 1.5 million native plants have been planted, and more than 2,000 acres are under restoration, earning a UN
Article Text:
Image courtesy of Green Seattle Partners

How a community came together to restore Seattle's urban forests

Image courtesy of Green Seattle Partners

From neglected parklands to a restoration success story

Image courtesy of Green Seattle Partners

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

A forest does not need to be replanted from scratch to be brought back to life. Sometimes, all it takes is a little collective effort and a community willing to restore what has been neglected. We saw during COVID-19 how reduced human activity made some environmental changes more visible: birds returned, animals were spotted in cities, fish swam in rivers where people had once hesitated to dip their feet, and mountains became visible from miles away.In Seattle, thousands of volunteers have spent the past two decades doing exactly that: not starting something new, but saving what is already there. What began in 2005 as an effort to revive neglected urban forests has grown into a major restoration initiative, with more than 1.5 million native plants planted and over 2,000 acres brought under restoration. The work has now earned the city a United Nations honour.According to the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP), the Green Seattle Partnership has been recognised as a World Restoration Flagship under the UN Decade on Ecosystem Restoration, following two decades of community-led efforts to revive the city's neglected urban forests.Seattle Mayor Katie B. Wilson said in a statement published by the UN Decade, “Through partnership, community stewardship of Seattle’s forested parklands has blossomed.”She also said, “We are honored to share the successful effort and our continued learning with cities around the world as part of the World Restoration Flagship programme.”The Green Seattle Partnership was launched in 2005 as a collaboration between the City of Seattle and the community to address the deteriorating condition of its urban forests. Over the years, many of the city's forested parklands had been affected by invasive plant species, declining native vegetation and a lack of regular maintenance. These changes threatened the natural habitats of local wildlife and the ecological health of the forests.Rather than treating forest restoration as the sole responsibility of government agencies, the initiative brought together residents, volunteers, environmental organisations and city departments. People began coming forward voluntarily and dedicating their time to the cause. And this shows something very profound: everything is not the government's responsibility. The city is ours too, and looking after it is our duty just as much as it is the government's.The partnership also focused on ensuring that restoration was not a one-time activity. Volunteers continued returning to the same sites to maintain the newly planted vegetation and prevent invasive species from taking over again. This long-term approach helped transform the initiative from a city-led environmental programme into a community-driven effort.“I set out alone toward my destination, yet people kept joining in, and a caravan was formed.” Legendary Urdu poet Majrooh Sultanpuri wrote these words, and that is what happened in Seattle. Over the years, thousands of residents came forward and contributed their time and effort to the programme, demonstrating how collective participation can help protect and restore natural spaces within a growing city.What makes it remarkable is not just the number of plants it has introduced, but the scale of the restoration work carried out over the years. According to the partnership's 20-year report, more than 2,032 acres of land across over 230 parks were under active restoration as of September 2025. The initiative had also recorded more than 1.5 million native plants planted, including over 355,000 trees.The contribution of volunteers has been equally significant. Since its launch in 2005, the partnership has received more than 1.4 million hours of volunteer work, with young people accounting for approximately 23 per cent of the total. It has also trained nearly 500 volunteer Forest Stewards, who organise restoration activities and encourage residents to take responsibility for the natural spaces in their neighbourhoods.Seattle's Green Seattle Partnership shows how the restoration of nature does not always require grand projects or large-scale interventions. Sometimes, all it takes is a small initiative and a sense of togetherness to make a big difference.It all begins with people coming together to protect what already exists and ensure that it continues to thrive. What started as an effort to revive neglected urban forests has, over two decades, grown into a movement involving thousands of residents and millions of native plants. Its recognition by the United Nations is not just an honour for Seattle, but also an example of how community participation can play a vital role in restoring urban ecosystems. As cities continue to expand, the initiative offers an important reminder that development and nature need not always come at the expense of one another.
Article Summary: Seattle's Green Seattle Partnership shows how the restoration of nature does not always require grand projects or large-scale interventions. What started as an effort to revive neglected urban forests has grown into a major restoration initiative, with more than 1.5 million native plants planted. The work has now earned the city a United Nations honour.

Article Title: ‘Transparency is key’: Ex-White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt urges Trump team to address US tech outages

Karoline Leavitt.

Former White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt has urged the Trump administration to be more transparent about a series of technology outages that have disrupted air travel, banking and other services across the US, saying even she is worried about the situation.“I’m checking my bank account with a little bit of worry,” Leavitt said during an appearance on Fox News' 'Fox & Friends'. “Transparency is key.”Leavitt, who stepped down as White House press secretary in August, said she was now experiencing the disruptions as an ordinary American, without access to classified government briefings.“I’m one of those Americans now, right? No longer serving in government, no longer getting those classified briefings about what’s really going on behind the scenes,” she said.According to the New York Post, Leavitt called on the White House to issue a direct message to Americans when President Donald Trump returns from his overseas trip. She said either Trump or another administration official should explain what the government knows about the outages.Leavitt described the situation as one that had been “spiraling for quite some time” and said concerns had spread on social media, particularly TikTok.She added that friends had also been contacting her to ask what was happening.She also referred to Vice President JD Vance's recent remarks that he did not anticipate a crisis, saying the administration should communicate that reassurance to the public “wide and loud”.The outages have affected several major sectors in recent days. On Friday, the Federal Aviation Administration imposed a nationwide ground stop that halted flights across US airports for more than four hours. The disruption was attributed to problems involving routers in the air traffic control system.Microsoft services, including Outlook and Teams, also experienced global disruptions last week, while customers of major banks, including JPMorgan Chase, Bank of America, and Wells Fargo, reported difficulties accessing their accounts on Monday.Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin suggested that superintelligence could be behind the disruptions but said he was 98 per cent certain they were not linked to a cyberattack.Trump, meanwhile, played down concerns on Tuesday, saying the outages were part of the problems that could occur in a large and powerful country.“It’s life. When you’re big and powerful and have all the money, things like that happen,” he said.During the Fox News appearance, Leavitt also addressed speculation about Vance's political future, saying she believed him when he said he had not yet decided whether to run for president in 2028.
Article Summary: Former White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt says she is 'worried' about technology outages. She called on the White House to issue a direct message to Americans when President Donald Trump returns from his overseas trip. She also referred to Vice President JD Vance's recent remarks that he did not anticipate a crisis.

Article Title: Florida man grabs invasive python in Everglades National Park thinking he is protecting wildlife, gets $180 fine and ranger warnings; his legal battle ends with the citation being dropped
Article Text:

A trip through Everglades National Park took an unexpected turn for Yatir Nitzany when he came across an invasive Burmese python and decided to catch it himself. The encounter, which was recorded on camera, later brought him into conflict with federal park regulations. Although Florida authorities have encouraged efforts to remove invasive species, handling wildlife inside a national park comes with different restrictions. According to NBC6 South Florida, Nitzany received a $180 citation from a park ranger for taking hold of the snake. Months of uncertainty over the penalty eventually led him to federal court, where the case was dismissed on Friday. The decision, however, left him without a clear explanation of why the citation had been withdrawn.Nitzany said he had not set out on a dedicated python-hunting trip when he encountered the snake. It crossed his path during his visit to Everglades National Park, prompting him to intervene. He argued that Burmese pythons pose a serious threat to the area's wildlife and that removing one from the environment was the right thing to do.The invasive snakes have become a major concern in South Florida, where their presence has affected native animal populations.Burmese pythons are non-native predators that feed on a wide range of mammals and birds. Their ability to establish themselves in the Everglades has made controlling their numbers a continuing challenge for wildlife authorities.Speaking about his decision to grab the animal, Nitzany pointed to the damage he believed the species was causing. He said the snakes had become dominant predators in the ecosystem, affecting the natural balance between native species.Nitzany's attempt to handle the python brought him into contact with federal park regulations. A ranger issued him a citation carrying a $180 penalty for handling wildlife on federal land without authorisation.The distinction between removing an invasive animal and handling wildlife inside a national park became central to the dispute. Florida has programmes that allow trained participants and members of the public to help remove invasive pythons from designated areas. Those arrangements do not automatically extend to national parks, where separate federal rules govern interactions with wildlife.Nitzany disputed the penalty, saying he did not believe his actions amounted to wrongdoing. He questioned why someone attempting to remove an invasive species should face a fine, particularly when the animal was considered harmful to the surrounding environment.When the matter reached federal court, Nitzany was accompanied by wildlife advocate Ron Magill. The two were prepared to challenge the citation and explain the environmental problems associated with Burmese pythons in the Everglades.The hearing ended with the citation being dismissed. However, Nitzany said he and Magill were not given a detailed account of the grounds for the decision. According to Nitzany, they were simply told that the citation had been written incorrectly.The dismissal brought an end to the immediate dispute over the $180 penalty, but it did not settle the wider question of whether members of the public should be allowed to intervene when they encounter invasive species inside federal parks.Nitzany also described receiving text messages and voicemail recordings from park rangers during the period before the court appearance. He said the communications made him uncomfortable, particularly because they referred to the possibility of a federal bench warrant if he failed to appear.In one recorded message, a ranger warned that the matter could be taken before a judge and that a warrant might be requested if Nitzany did not attend court. He interpreted the warning as pressure to settle the citation by paying the fine.Asked whether the communication had felt threatening, Nitzany said he was concerned by the possibility of facing further legal consequences over a penalty he believed was unjustified. The issue became another part of his account of how the citation had been handled.Magill said the case had drawn attention to a difference between Florida's approach to invasive species and the restrictions operating on federal land. While state-level initiatives encourage the removal of Burmese pythons in authorised circumstances, national park regulations place limits on what visitors can do when they encounter wildlife. He said he wanted to push for a change that would allow an exception for people attempting to remove invasive animals, rather than penalising them for intervening.His proposed change would need to account for the particular rules governing national parks and ensure that any removal activity could be carried out safely and appropriately.The National Park Service and the US Attorney's Office were contacted by NBC6 for comment. The broadcaster sought clarification about the reason for the dismissal and whether park rangers routinely contact people who receive citations. Neither office had responded at the time of its report. For Nitzany, the court's decision meant he no longer had to contest the $180 penalty. The broader disagreement over how visitors should respond to invasive pythons on federal land, however, remained unresolved.
Article Summary: Yatir Nitzany came across an invasive Burmese python in Everglades National Park and decided to remove it himself. Article Title: Hawaii created a 74-acre artificial reef off Oʻahu; within 2–3 years, mean fish biomass was reported to be 20 times higher, and the average number of species had risen fivefold
Article Text:
Artificial reefs can turn bare seabed into a home for fish (representative image). Image Credits: ChatGPT

From bare sand to a bustling reef

A big jump in just a few years

Sunken structures can become homes for marine life. Here, fish crowd around the City of Houston wreck off North Carolina. Image Credit: John McCord, Coastal Studies Institute via NOAA

Why fish move in

It's not all good news

The road ahead

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Why it matters

Imagine a patch of seabed that looks like a desert. It has flat sand, bare limestone, and hardly any fish. Now imagine the same site a few years later, but teeming with life. That's what happened on an artificial reef off the coast of Oʻahu, Hawaii. The amount of fish in the area increased dramatically within two to three years of deployment, according to a NOAA-hosted presentation by Paul Murakawa of Hawaii’s Division of Aquatic Resources.The reef sits in Maunalua Bay, off Kahala on Oʻahu. It covers about 74 acres, or about 30 hectares, and has been in place for quite some time. According to Hawaii's Division of Aquatic Resources , the first artificial reef in Hawaii was built in 1961, and that reef is the one at Maunalua Bay. That's more than 60 years ago. Before the structures went down, the site was barren, made up only of bare limestone and sand. Murakawa’s presentation puts the average biomass of fish in that area at merely 5.4 grams per square metre. Biomass is basically the weight of the fish in that place. The average number of species identified was just seven.Then came the change. Mean biomass increased 20-fold within two to three years post-deployment.The average number of species rose fivefold. That's a lot of numbers in a short span of time. In plain terms, the area had many more fish by weight and many more kinds of fish. For a spot that started out as bare limestone and sand, that was quite a turnaround. More reefs came in the decades after 1961 on both Oʻahu and Maui, according to the state's reef programme page. So, Maunalua Bay is actually part of a longer story rather than just a one-off experiment.Fish need homes to live. A flat, open seabed without any structures in sight doesn't do the trick. The Hawaii reef programme places structures that help make the habitat better in areas that lack natural structure. More habitat can mean more fish. Murakawa shows that the use of artificial reefs can reduce fishing and diving pressure on the natural reefs. This might allow the natural reefs to have some breathing room. The presentation also mentions fishing opportunities and tourism spots in the overview of Hawaii's artificial reefs. So, the benefits can be enjoyed by people as well as fish.The same presentation lists some drawbacks. Artificial reefs can be fish aggregation areas. Researchers and fishers often debate whether the reefs merely attract the existing fish rather than add to the overall fish population. Fish gathered around a structure can also be easier to catch, which can add to fishing pressure. The headline numbers also have a catch. They are averages from a single example, published in a presentation rather than a peer-reviewed paper. They look promising, but that doesn't prove that all artificial reefs will do the same.Murakawa identifies three main issues and lessons learnt: permit process, type of material and the need for a complete assessment. He wants a better permit process between federal and state agencies down the road. His list of priorities also includes the use of artificial reefs as compensatory mitigation. That's a formal way of saying a reef could be created to compensate for environmental damage elsewhere. The programme also uses donated materials.As stated on the state reef programme website, such donations help the programme use non-state money to match federal Sport Fish Restoration funding.Artificial reefs aren't a replacement for protecting natural ones, and the presentation doesn't suggest that they are. However, the Maunalua Bay example shows what can happen when a bare patch of seabed gets some structures on it. In a few years, it went from sparse to a much busier and livelier habitat. For a world that often hears bad news about the oceans, this might be something worth knowing.
Article Summary: Artificial reefs can turn bare seabed into a home for fish. The amount of fish in the area increased dramatically within two to three years of deployment. The first artificial reef in Hawaii was built in 1961, and that reef is the one at Maunalua Bay.

Article Title: A 24-year-old was shot dead by a security guard at a San Francisco Walgreens after an alleged shoplifting incident; his family has reached a $5 million settlement with the guard and his employer

The family of Banko Brown, a 24-year-old Black transgender man fatally shot by a security guard at a Walgreens store in San Francisco in 2023, has reached a $5 million settlement with the guard and his employer. The agreement resolves the wrongful death claims against security guard Michael Earl-Wayne Anthony and Kingdom Group Protective Services, while the family’s legal battle against Walgreens and Allied Universal Security Services remains ongoing. The development was reported by KQED, SFGATE and Bay City News. Brown was killed on April 27, 2023, at a Walgreens store on Market Street in downtown San Francisco. He was allegedly attempting to leave the store with stolen snacks when he was confronted by Anthony, who was working as an armed security guard for Kingdom Group. According to reports and footage of the incident, an altercation followed inside the store, during which Anthony restrained Brown in a chokehold-like manoeuvre. Brown eventually managed to get back on his feet, picked up his bag and began walking towards the exit. Anthony then fired a single shot at him as he was moving away from the store. Brown, who was unarmed, died from his injuries. No weapon was recovered from the scene or his belongings.Brown’s parents, Terry Brown and Kevinisha Henderson, filed a wrongful death lawsuit in 2023 against Anthony, Kingdom Group Protective Services, Walgreens and Allied Universal Security Services. The family alleged that inadequate security practices, training and supervision contributed to the fatal encounter.The $5 million settlement was disclosed in a motion filed in San Francisco Superior Court on November 12, 2026. Ben Nisenbaum, the attorney representing Brown’s family, confirmed that both sides had agreed to the arrangement. Under the settlement terms, the complaint against Anthony and Kingdom Group will be dismissed. However, the agreement does not bring the wider legal dispute to an end. Claims against Walgreens, its parent company Walgreens Boots Alliance, and Allied Universal Security Services are still pending.Court documents have also brought attention to the circumstances surrounding the shooting. According to reporting by Bay City News, a Kingdom Group executive acknowledged that Walgreens management at individual stores had frequently pressured security officers to act beyond the company’s policies. An email included in the court records indicated that security guards at Northern California Walgreens locations had been instructed to begin stopping suspected shoplifters approximately two weeks before Brown’s death. Another detail that emerged from the legal proceedings was that Anthony, who joined Kingdom Group in 2022, had reportedly received his security guard training through online sessions.Brown’s death triggered protests and widespread criticism, particularly from civil rights and transgender advocacy groups. His killing also prompted renewed scrutiny of the use of armed security personnel in retail stores and the extent to which guards should be permitted to physically intervene in suspected thefts.San Francisco District Attorney Brooke Jenkins declined to file criminal charges against Anthony, citing insufficient evidence to establish that he had committed a crime. Anthony had told investigators that he feared for his safety during the confrontation. California Attorney General Rob Bonta subsequently reviewed the district attorney’s decision and concluded that Jenkins had not abused her prosecutorial discretion.The incident also prompted changes to security practices in the city. Kingdom Group guards were disarmed at San Francisco Walgreens locations within days of the shooting, and the company was subsequently removed as the store’s contracted security provider. In October 2023, the San Francisco Board of Supervisors amended the city’s police code to restrict armed security guards from drawing their firearms to protect property alone.The revised rules require an actual threat to a person’s safety before a guard can draw a weapon. The latest settlement represents a significant development in the family’s civil case, but the unresolved claims against Walgreens and Allied Universal mean the legal proceedings surrounding Brown’s death are not yet over.
